subject: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug

messages.author: 979e6ae871655730
messages.subject: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug
parts:
Dear all, 

I've discovered what I think is a bug in ggplot2's use of geom_text and am wondering if anyone out there has a work-around/is able to point out what I'm doing wrong. 

Consider the following sample code: 

library(ggplot2)

Treatment <- rep(c('C','T'),3)
Group <- rep(c('A','B','C'),each=2)
Response <- c(0.22894321, 0.23391813, 0.92256514, 0.92705167, 0.05982670, 0.09667674)
Differences <- c('+0pts',  '+0pts', '+0pts', '+0pts', '+4pts', '+4pts')

df <- data.frame(Treatment, Group, Response, Differences)

ydef <- c(0.03, 0.03, 0.2)

hist <- ggplot(df, aes(x=Group, y=Response, fill=Treatment, stat="identity"))
hist + geom_bar(position = "dodge")  + geom_text(aes(label = Differences,y=ydef))

If this works for you the same way that it does for me--using the most current versions of ggplot2 and R 2.12.2--groups B and C should have two text floats each, spaced equal distances apart. Obviously this is not what we want. Now change 'ydef' such that

ydef <- c(0.03, 0.03, 0.03)

re-run the script above, and the problem is solved--each group now only has one text float corresponding to differences (or rather two, layered exactly on top of each other). How does this make any sense? I've been using this basic structure in a fairly large scale application, and have not had any trouble until I got to this specific example with these specific numbers.

Part of the problem may be the way I'm constructing 'Differences', by adding it as a column to the data frame and placing this text on the chart with geom_text. If there was a way to do the same thing using a vector with only three character entries I'm sure that would solve the problem. 

In short (1) help please! and (2) here is a potentially interesting bug for the consideration of the ggplot2 community. 

Cheers, 
Aaron

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug
parts:
Hi:

It's not really a bug but rather one of the nuances of ggplot2 that's
bitten you.

If you do this:

# Create a separate data frame for the text
df2 <- data.frame(Group = factor(LETTERS[1:3]),
ydef = c(0.03, 0.03, 0.20),
Differences = c('+0pts', '+0pts', '+4pts'),
stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# notice the classes and compare to df
str(df2)

# Modify the plot call:
hist <- ggplot(df)
hist + geom_bar(aes(x=Group, y=Response, fill=Treatment, stat="identity"),
position = 'dodge') +
geom_text(data = df2, aes(x = Group, y = ydef, label = Differences))

It works as expected. The nuance is that the aesthetics you define in
ggplot() are expected to be present in every layer [geom]. It is often
the case that when geom_text() is one of the layers, you don't want
all the aesthetics (and all sets of values) in the original data
frame. In your case, the Treatment variable adds duplication to the
Differences. The 'solution' is to decouple the aesthetics needed in
the bar chart from those needed in the labels; one way to do that is
to create separate data frames for the two tasks, passing the
aesthetics information to the geoms rather than to ggplot() and
realizing that you can use different data frames in different layers.
[This is the nuance. :)]

By creating a separate data frame for the labels (x, y, label), you
can decouple the data used to produce the bar chart layer from that to
produce the text labels. When using different data sets in different
layers, you eventually learn (from getting your head beaten in by
ggplot2 :) to make the ggplot() statement as minimal as possible; this
is why you'll see examples where ggplot() is called without any
arguments and the data frames and aesthetics are passed to the
individual geoms. This also would have worked:

hist <- ggplot()
hist + geom_bar(data = df, aes(x=Group, y=Response, fill=Treatment,
stat="identity"),
position = 'dodge') +
geom_text(data = df2, aes(x = Group, y = ydef, label = Differences))

Also notice I use the same variable name for x in each layer but
different y variables.

Admittedly, you don't see many examples of this in the on-line help,
but there are several such examples in the group archives, although
you may have to dig a bit to find them. This behavior isn't 'obvious',
but learning this little nugget about ggplot2 can be very beneficial
down the road.

HTH,
Dennis
